chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Abu Hamza, from Al-Abd Al-Salih (peace be upon him), who said:

A mother of a child of his son asked him, saying, 'May I be sacrificed for you! I wish to ask you about something, but I am shy to do so.' He said, 'Ask, and do not be shy.' She said, 'Menstrual blood struck my garment, so I washed it, but its trace did not disappear.' So he said, 'Dye it with red pigment (mishq) until it mixes and the trace disappears.'

key_terms.أُمُّ وَلَدٍ: Mother of a child (concubine or female slave who bore a child)
key_terms.يَخْتَلِطَ: It mixes/merges (referring to the trace blending with the dye)

ai.seo_question: How to purify clothes stained with menstrual blood when washing leaves a visible trace?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the practical flexibility in Shia jurisprudence regarding ritual purity, where the removal of the physical substance (al-ayn) is prioritized over the complete elimination of its visual trace. The Imam’s instruction to dye the garment with 'mishq' (a red dye) illustrates the principle that if the stain's color blends with the fabric, it is no longer considered an impediment to prayer, reflecting a pragmatic approach to daily worship. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on ease and the removal of hardship in matters of taharah.
